name: Mongol conquests
summary: Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and launched campaigns that his sons and grandsons carried from Korea and China to Russia, Poland, Hungary and the Middle East. Mobile horse archers, captured siege engineers and deliberate terror built the largest contiguous land empire in history, though Mamluk Egypt, Japan, Dai Viet and Java held them off. The conquests killed millions but also tied East and West together through trade along the Silk Road.

steps.label: 1206 to 1215
steps.title: Genghis Khan turns on China
steps.text: Temujin was proclaimed Genghis Khan in 1206 and forced Western Xia to submit by 1210. In 1211 he invaded the Jurchen Jin empire of northern China, breaking its main army at Yehuling, and in 1215 the Jin capital Zhongdu near modern Beijing fell and was sacked.

events.name: Battle of Yehuling
events.text: The Mongols routed the main Jin field army at the Badger Mouth pass.

events.name: Fall of Zhongdu
events.text: The Jin capital near modern Beijing fell and was sacked after a long blockade.

steps.label: 1219 to 1223
steps.title: Destruction of Khwarazm
steps.text: When the Khwarazm Shah's governor at Otrar massacred a Mongol caravan and its envoys, Genghis Khan marched west with perhaps 100,000 riders. Bukhara, Samarkand, Urgench, Merv and Nishapur fell one after another, Jalal al-Din was beaten on the Indus, and Jebe and Subutai rode round the Caspian to crush the Rus and Cumans on the Kalka.

moves.label: Main army via Otrar to Bukhara and Samarkand
Pursuit of Jalal al-Din to the Indus

events.name: Fall of Samarkand
events.text: The great Khwarazmian city surrendered after a short siege and was plundered.

events.name: Battle of the Indus
events.text: Genghis Khan destroyed Jalal al-Din's army, though the prince escaped by swimming the river.

events.name: Battle of the Kalka River
events.text: Jebe and Subutai crushed an army of Rus princes and Cumans in their first clash with Europe.

steps.label: 1227 to 1234
steps.title: Fall of Xia and Jin
steps.text: Western Xia was annihilated in 1227, the year Genghis Khan died during the campaign. His son and successor Ogedei renewed the war on the Jin while Tolui swung through Song territory to take the Jin from behind, and in 1234 the last Jin emperor died at Caizhou, besieged by Mongols and their Song allies.

moves.label: Main army across the Yellow River

events.name: Fall of Western Xia
events.text: The Xia capital surrendered and its people were massacred as Genghis Khan lay dying.

events.name: Battle of Sanfengshan
events.text: Tolui destroyed the last great Jin field army in a snowstorm.

events.name: Siege of Caizhou
events.text: Mongols and Song allies took the last Jin refuge, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 1237 to 1242
steps.title: Rus, Poland and Hungary
steps.text: Batu and Subutai led the western campaign, conquering the Volga Bulgars and destroying the principalities of Rus, sacking Ryazan, Vladimir and Kiev. In 1241 one column smashed the Poles and Silesians at Legnica while the main army annihilated the Hungarians at Mohi, but news of Ogedei's death in 1242 drew the Mongols back to the steppe.

events.name: Siege of Kiev
events.text: The Mongols stormed and devastated the old capital of Rus.

events.name: Battle of Legnica
events.text: A Mongol column destroyed the army of Duke Henry II of Silesia.

events.name: Battle of Mohi
events.text: Batu and Subutai annihilated the army of King Bela IV of Hungary.

steps.label: 1256 to 1260
steps.title: Baghdad and Ain Jalut
steps.text: Great Khan Mongke sent his brother Hulagu west. He destroyed the Assassin castles of Alamut and in 1258 sacked Baghdad, killing the last Abbasid caliph, then took Aleppo and Damascus. When Hulagu withdrew most of his army, the Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz and Baibars destroyed the force left under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut, and the Euphrates became the frontier.

events.name: Siege of Baghdad
events.text: Hulagu sacked the Abbasid capital and ended five centuries of the caliphate there.

events.name: Battle of Ain Jalut
events.text: The Mamluks dealt the Mongols their first great defeat and saved Egypt.

steps.label: 1268 to 1279
steps.title: Kublai conquers the Song
steps.text: Kublai Khan, who founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, besieged the twin river fortresses of Xiangyang and Fancheng for five years until Persian counterweight trebuchets broke them. Bayan then drove down the Yangtze to take the Song capital Lin'an in 1276, and the last Song loyalists were destroyed at sea off Yamen in 1279.

events.name: Siege of Xiangyang
events.text: The fall of the key Song fortress opened the Yangtze to the Mongols.

events.name: Fall of Lin'an
events.text: The Song court surrendered its capital to Bayan without a fight.

events.name: Battle of Yamen
events.text: The Yuan fleet destroyed the last Song court and fleet, ending the dynasty.

steps.label: 1274 and 1281
steps.title: The invasions of Japan
steps.text: By now the empire had split into four khanates, but Kublai still sought new conquests. His Mongol, Chinese and Korean fleets landed at Hakata Bay in 1274 and again in 1281, when the Japanese had built a stone wall along the shore; both times the samurai held the beaches and typhoons, the kamikaze or divine wind, wrecked the fleets.

events.name: First invasion, Hakata Bay
events.text: The invaders won ashore but re-embarked and lost many ships to a storm.

events.name: Second invasion and the kamikaze
events.text: A typhoon destroyed the huge combined fleet sheltering off Takashima.

steps.label: 1277 to 1294
steps.title: The limits of conquest
steps.text: In Southeast Asia the Yuan broke the kingdom of Pagan in Burma, but Dai Viet under Tran Hung Dao defeated three invasions, the last on the stakes of the Bach Dang river in 1288. A fleet sent to punish Java in 1293 was turned on and driven out by Raden Wijaya, founder of Majapahit, and when Kublai died in 1294 the age of Mongol expansion was over.

events.name: Fall of Pagan
events.text: The Yuan invasion shattered the Pagan kingdom, which broke into rival states.

events.name: Battle of Bach Dang
events.text: Tran Hung Dao trapped the Yuan fleet on iron-tipped stakes planted in the river.

events.name: Mongol expedition to Java
events.text: Raden Wijaya used the Mongols to defeat Kediri, then attacked and drove them out.

name: Edward I's conquest of Wales
summary: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, Prince of Wales, ruled most of Wales from his mountain heartland of Gwynedd until he refused homage to Edward I of England. Two English invasions, in 1277 and 1282 to 1283, used sea power and slow coastal advances to strangle Gwynedd, and Llywelyn's death at Orewin Bridge ended independent Welsh rule. Edward secured the conquest with the Statute of Rhuddlan and a ring of great stone castles.

steps.title: The first war
steps.text: Llywelyn refused to do homage, and Edward attacked from three directions: Mortimer from the Marches, Payn de Chaworth in the south, and the king himself along the north coast from Chester, building roads and forts as he went. His fleet seized Anglesey and its harvest, the breadbasket of Gwynedd, and the starving Welsh accepted the Treaty of Aberconwy, which confined Llywelyn to Gwynedd west of the Conwy.

moves.label: Royal army along the north coast

events.name: Treaty of Aberconwy
events.text: Llywelyn kept his title but lost everything east of the Conwy and paid heavy fines.

steps.title: Revolt and the death of Llywelyn
steps.text: On Palm Sunday 1282 Llywelyn's brother Dafydd stormed Hawarden castle, and all of Wales rose. Edward advanced again along the coast, but Luke de Tany's force crossing a bridge of boats from Anglesey was destroyed at Moel-y-Don. Llywelyn then went south to raise mid Wales, and on 11 December he was killed near Builth at Orewin Bridge.

moves.label: Royal army to Rhuddlan and the Conwy
Bridge of boats over the Menai

events.name: Attack on Hawarden
events.text: Dafydd's surprise attack on the English castle began the final war.

events.name: Battle of Moel-y-Don
events.text: The Welsh routed an English force crossing the Menai Strait.

events.name: Battle of Orewin Bridge
events.text: Llywelyn, the last native Prince of Wales, was killed and his army broken.

steps.label: 1283 to 1284
steps.title: Gwynedd falls
steps.text: Edward kept campaigning through the winter. His armies took Dolwyddelan, the Earl of Pembroke captured Castell y Bere, and Dafydd was hunted down in the mountains in June 1283 and executed at Shrewsbury. The Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 annexed the principality to the English crown, guarded by new castles at Conwy, Caernarfon and Harlech.

moves.label: From Aberystwyth to Castell y Bere

events.name: Siege of Castell y Bere
events.text: The last major Welsh castle surrendered in April 1283.

events.name: Capture of Dafydd
events.text: Betrayed and captured near Bera Mawr, Dafydd was executed for treason.

events.name: Statute of Rhuddlan
events.text: Wales was annexed and divided into English-style shires.

name: Hundred Years' War
summary: The English Plantagenet kings fought the French Valois kings for over a century over English lands in France and Edward III's claim to the French crown. England won famous victories at Crecy, Poitiers and Agincourt and under Henry V held northern France, but Joan of Arc and a reformed French army with powerful artillery drove the English out of everything except Calais. The war forged national identities in both countries and helped end the age of the armoured knight.

steps.label: 1337 to 1340
steps.title: War at sea
steps.text: Philip VI confiscated Edward III's duchy of Aquitaine in 1337, and Edward answered by claiming the French crown through his mother. The first great clash came at sea: in 1340 the English fleet caught the French navy packed in the harbour of Sluys and destroyed it, winning control of the Channel for the invasions to come.

events.name: Battle of Sluys
events.text: English archers and men-at-arms destroyed the French fleet at anchor.

steps.label: 1346 to 1347
steps.title: Crecy and Calais
steps.text: Edward III landed in Normandy, sacked Caen and marched toward Flanders with Philip VI in pursuit. At Crecy the English longbowmen shattered wave after wave of French cavalry, and Edward went on to take Calais after an eleven-month siege; England would hold it for two centuries.

events.name: Battle of Crecy
events.text: English longbows and dismounted knights crushed the French army.

events.name: Siege of Calais
events.text: Calais surrendered after an eleven-month siege.

steps.label: 1355 to 1360
steps.title: Poitiers and Bretigny
steps.text: Edward the Black Prince led destructive raids from English Gascony. Caught near Poitiers by King John II, he won a crushing victory and captured the French king, and the Treaty of Bretigny in 1360 gave England a greatly enlarged, fully sovereign Aquitaine.

events.name: Battle of Poitiers
events.text: The Black Prince defeated and captured John II of France.

events.name: Treaty of Bretigny
events.text: Edward dropped his claim to the crown in exchange for a sovereign Aquitaine and Calais.

steps.label: 1369 to 1380
steps.title: The French recovery
steps.text: Charles V renewed the war and, guided by Bertrand du Guesclin, avoided pitched battles while retaking towns one by one. A Castilian fleet allied to France destroyed an English fleet off La Rochelle in 1372, English raids marched through empty countryside, and by 1380 England held little beyond Calais and the coast from Bordeaux to Bayonne.

events.name: Battle of La Rochelle
events.text: A Castilian fleet allied to France destroyed an English fleet and its pay chests.

steps.label: 1415 to 1420
steps.title: Agincourt and Troyes
steps.text: Henry V revived the war while France was torn by civil war between Armagnacs and Burgundians. After taking Harfleur he marched for Calais and won an astonishing victory at Agincourt, then conquered Normandy, and with Burgundy now his ally the Treaty of Troyes in 1420 made him heir to the French throne.

events.name: Battle of Agincourt
events.text: Henry V's archers destroyed a much larger French army in the mud.

events.name: Treaty of Troyes
events.text: Charles VI disinherited his son and named Henry V heir to France.

steps.label: 1428 to 1429
steps.title: Joan of Arc
steps.text: The English and Burgundians held all of northern France and besieged Orleans, the gateway to the south still loyal to the Dauphin Charles. Joan of Arc helped lift the siege in nine days, the French routed the English at Patay, and Charles was crowned at Reims, turning the tide of the war.

moves.label: March to the coronation at Reims

events.name: Siege of Orleans
events.text: Joan of Arc's relief force broke the English siege.

events.name: Battle of Patay
events.text: French cavalry caught the English archers before they could deploy and captured Talbot.

events.name: Coronation at Reims
events.text: Charles VII was crowned, undermining the English claim.

steps.label: 1435 to 1450
steps.title: Normandy lost
steps.text: Burgundy made peace with Charles VII at Arras in 1435 and Paris returned to France the next year. Charles built a standing army and a powerful artillery train under the Bureau brothers, and in 1449 to 1450 reconquered Normandy, destroying the last English relief army at Formigny.

events.name: Peace of Arras
events.text: Burgundy abandoned the English alliance and reconciled with Charles VII.

events.name: Battle of Formigny
events.text: French troops and cannon destroyed the English relief army in Normandy.

steps.label: 1451 to 1453
steps.title: Castillon
steps.text: French armies overran Gascony in 1451, ending three centuries of English rule in Bordeaux. The townspeople invited the English back, but in 1453 John Talbot attacked the French artillery camp at Castillon and was killed with much of his army, and Bordeaux surrendered for good. Only Calais remained English.

events.name: Battle of Castillon
events.text: French artillery killed Talbot and broke the last English army in Gascony.

events.name: Surrender of Bordeaux
events.text: The fall of Bordeaux ended the war, leaving England only Calais.

name: Rise of the Ottoman Empire
summary: From a small frontier principality in northwest Anatolia, the Ottoman dynasty crossed into Europe in 1354 and over the next two centuries conquered the Balkans, Constantinople, Syria, Egypt and Hungary. Disciplined Janissary infantry, early mastery of gunpowder and capable sultans overcame Serbs, crusaders, Byzantines, Mamluks and Hungarians, surviving even a crushing defeat by Timur in 1402. The advance was finally checked at the walls of Vienna in 1529.

steps.label: 1354 to 1371
steps.title: Crossing into Europe
steps.text: Orhan's Ottomans, already masters of Bithynia, crossed the Dardanelles as mercenaries in Byzantine civil wars, and in 1354 his son Suleyman Pasha occupied Gallipoli after an earthquake ruined its walls. Murad I pushed into Thrace, made Adrianople (Edirne) his base, and in 1371 destroyed the Serbian lords on the Maritsa.

events.name: Gallipoli taken
events.text: The Ottomans gained their first permanent foothold in Europe.

events.name: Edirne taken
events.text: Adrianople became the Ottoman capital in Europe.

events.name: Battle of the Maritsa
events.text: Murad's forces annihilated the army of the Serbian despots in Macedonia.

steps.title: Kosovo
steps.text: Murad I marched up the Balkan valleys against Prince Lazar of Serbia and his allies. On the Field of Blackbirds both rulers died, Murad stabbed by a Serbian noble and Lazar executed after the battle, but the Ottoman army held the field and Serbia became a tributary vassal under Murad's son Bayezid I.

moves.label: Up the Maritsa and Morava valleys

events.name: Battle of Kosovo
events.text: Both rulers died, but Serbia's power was broken and it became an Ottoman vassal.

steps.label: 1393 to 1396
steps.title: Nicopolis
steps.text: Bayezid I, called the Thunderbolt, annexed Bulgaria in 1393 and began blockading Constantinople. King Sigismund of Hungary led a great crusade of Hungarians, French and Burgundian knights down the Danube, but at Nicopolis the reckless French charge broke on Ottoman stakes and infantry and Bayezid destroyed the crusade.

events.name: Conquest of Tarnovo
events.text: The Bulgarian capital fell and Bulgaria was annexed.

events.name: Battle of Nicopolis
events.text: Bayezid destroyed the largest crusade of the age.

steps.label: 1402 to 1413
steps.title: Ankara and the Interregnum
steps.text: Bayezid's expansion into eastern Anatolia collided with Timur. At Ankara in 1402 the Anatolian vassals deserted, Timur crushed the Ottoman army and captured the sultan, who died in captivity. Bayezid's sons fought a decade-long civil war until Mehmed I reunited the state in 1413.

events.name: Battle of Ankara
events.text: Timur destroyed the Ottoman army and took Bayezid prisoner.

events.name: Ottoman Interregnum ends
events.text: Mehmed I defeated his brothers and restored a single Ottoman state.

steps.label: 1443 to 1448
steps.title: Varna
steps.text: Under Murad II the empire recovered, and Hungary answered with new crusades led by the general John Hunyadi. In 1444 King Wladyslaw of Poland and Hungary marched to the Black Sea coast, but Murad hurried back from Anatolia and won at Varna, where the young king was killed; Hunyadi was beaten again at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448.

events.name: Battle of Varna
events.text: Murad II crushed the crusaders and King Wladyslaw was killed.

events.name: Second Battle of Kosovo
events.text: Hunyadi's Hungarian army was defeated after three days of fighting.

steps.title: The fall of Constantinople
steps.text: Mehmed II built the fortress of Rumelihisari to close the Bosporus, then besieged Constantinople with some 80,000 men and enormous bombards. His ships were dragged overland into the Golden Horn, and on 29 May the Janissaries broke through the land walls; Constantine XI died in the fighting and the city became the Ottoman capital.

events.name: Siege of Constantinople
events.text: The thousand-year Byzantine Empire ended when the city fell on 29 May.

steps.label: 1456 to 1480
steps.title: Mehmed the Conqueror
steps.text: Hunyadi threw Mehmed back from Belgrade in 1456, holding the Danube for seventy years. Mehmed instead swallowed the remaining Balkan and Greek states: Serbia in 1459, the Byzantine Morea in 1460, Trebizond in 1461 and Bosnia in 1463, and in 1473 he defeated the eastern Turkmen ruler Uzun Hasan at Otlukbeli.

events.name: Siege of Belgrade
events.text: Hunyadi and the friar John of Capistrano broke the Ottoman siege.

events.name: Fall of Trebizond
events.text: The last Byzantine successor state surrendered to Mehmed.

events.name: Battle of Otlukbeli
events.text: Ottoman guns defeated Uzun Hasan and secured eastern Anatolia.

steps.label: 1514 to 1517
steps.title: Selim conquers the Middle East
steps.text: Selim I first crushed the new Safavid Shah Ismail at Chaldiran in 1514 with artillery and Janissary muskets. In 1516 he turned on the Mamluks, killing Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri at Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo, and in January 1517 took Cairo after victory at Ridaniya, making the Ottomans masters of Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia.

polities: Emirate of the White Sheep Turks

events.name: Battle of Chaldiran
events.text: Ottoman cannon and muskets routed Shah Ismail's cavalry.

events.name: Battle of Marj Dabiq
events.text: The Mamluk sultan was killed and Syria fell to the Ottomans.

events.name: Battle of Ridaniya
events.text: Selim took Cairo and ended the Mamluk Sultanate.

steps.label: 1521 to 1526
steps.title: Mohacs
steps.text: Suleiman the Magnificent took Belgrade, the key to Hungary, in 1521 and expelled the Knights of St John from Rhodes in 1522. In 1526 he marched up the Danube with about 60,000 men and at Mohacs annihilated the Hungarian army in under two hours; King Louis II drowned in the retreat, and the Hungarian kingdom split between rival claimants.

events.name: Fall of Belgrade
events.text: Suleiman took the fortress that had blocked the Ottomans since 1456.

events.name: Siege of Rhodes
events.text: The Knights of St John surrendered the island after a six-month siege.

events.name: Battle of Mohacs
events.text: The Hungarian army was destroyed and King Louis II was killed.

steps.title: The siege of Vienna
steps.text: Backing John Zapolya against the Habsburg Ferdinand I for the Hungarian crown, Suleiman retook Buda and pushed on to Vienna in September 1529. Heavy rains had forced him to leave his big guns behind, the garrison under Niklas Salm held the walls, and after three weeks and a failed final assault the Ottomans withdrew, marking the high-water mark of their advance in that era.

events.name: Buda retaken
events.text: Suleiman installed his vassal John Zapolya as king of Hungary.

events.name: Siege of Vienna
events.text: The defenders held, and the Ottomans withdrew before winter.

name: Timur's conquests
summary: Timur (Tamerlane), a Turkic-Mongol emir from near Samarkand, seized power in Transoxiana in 1370 and spent 35 years campaigning from Anatolia to India. He broke the Golden Horde, sacked Delhi, Baghdad and Damascus, and captured the Ottoman sultan at Ankara, killing perhaps millions along the way. His empire did not long survive him, but it crippled the Golden Horde and the Delhi Sultanate and gave the Ottomans a decade of civil war.

steps.label: 1360 to 1380
steps.title: Lord of Samarkand
steps.text: Timur, a minor noble of the Barlas tribe, rose through the chaotic wars of the western Chagatai Khanate. In 1370 he besieged his former ally Amir Husayn at Balkh, took power and made Samarkand his capital, ruling as emir in the name of puppet Chagatayid khans and spending the next decade subduing Khwarazm and Moghulistan.

events.name: Siege of Balkh
events.text: Timur defeated Amir Husayn and was proclaimed ruler of Transoxiana.

events.name: Fall of Urgench
events.text: Timur took the capital of Khwarazm after repeated campaigns.

steps.label: 1381 to 1387
steps.title: Conquest of Persia
steps.text: With Persia split among petty dynasties after the fall of the Ilkhanate, Timur took Herat in 1381 and swept west through Khorasan, Azerbaijan and Georgia. When Isfahan rebelled in 1387 his troops massacred its people and built towers of skulls. Meanwhile his former protege Tokhtamysh, now khan of the Golden Horde, sacked Tabriz and turned into his greatest rival.

events.name: Siege of Herat
events.text: The Kartid capital surrendered, opening Persia to Timur.

events.name: Sack of Tabriz
events.text: Tokhtamysh's raid on Tabriz began the war between the former allies.

events.name: Massacre of Isfahan
events.text: After a revolt Timur ordered the city's people killed, reportedly 70,000.

steps.label: 1391 to 1396
steps.title: Breaking the Golden Horde
steps.text: Timur marched across the steppe in 1391 and beat Tokhtamysh on the Kondurcha River near the Volga. When the khan struck again, Timur came through the Caucasus in 1395, crushed him on the Terek and then sacked the Horde's great trading cities of Sarai, Astrakhan and Tana, wrecking its economy for good; he came within reach of Moscow at Yelets before turning back.

events.name: Battle of the Kondurcha River
events.text: Timur defeated Tokhtamysh deep in the steppe.

events.name: Battle of the Terek River
events.text: Timur shattered the Golden Horde's main army.

events.name: Sack of Sarai
events.text: The Golden Horde capital was burned along with Astrakhan and Tana.

steps.label: 1398 to 1399
steps.title: The sack of Delhi
steps.text: Claiming the Delhi sultans were too tolerant of their Hindu subjects, Timur crossed the Hindu Kush and the Indus in 1398. Outside Delhi he had his Indian prisoners killed, beat Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud's army and its war elephants, and sacked the city for days before withdrawing with vast loot and craftsmen; the Delhi Sultanate never recovered its power.

moves.label: Over the Hindu Kush to Delhi

events.name: Battle of Delhi
events.text: Timur routed the sultan's army and sacked Delhi.

steps.label: 1399 to 1401
steps.title: Syria and Baghdad
steps.text: Timur's seven-year campaign in the west began against the Mamluk Sultanate. He stormed Aleppo in 1400, defeated the Mamluk army and took Damascus in 1401, carrying off its craftsmen to Samarkand, then returned east to storm rebellious Baghdad, where his soldiers were ordered to bring back heads.

events.name: Sack of Aleppo
events.text: Timur stormed the city after defeating its Mamluk garrison.

events.name: Fall of Damascus
events.text: The Mamluk sultan withdrew and Damascus was looted and burned.

events.name: Sack of Baghdad
events.text: Timur stormed Baghdad and massacred its people.

steps.title: Ankara
steps.text: The rivalry with Bayezid I came to a head when Timur marched into Anatolia. He outmanoeuvred the Ottoman army, cut it off from water near Ankara, and when the Anatolian vassals and Tatars changed sides he won a total victory and captured the sultan. He then took Smyrna from the Knights of St John and restored the Anatolian beyliks.

events.name: Battle of Ankara
events.text: Timur destroyed the Ottoman army and captured Bayezid.

events.name: Siege of Smyrna
events.text: Timur took the Hospitaller fortress in two weeks.

steps.label: 1404 to 1405
steps.title: The last campaign
steps.text: Back in Samarkand, the aged Timur gathered a great army to invade Ming China and set out in the depth of winter. He fell ill and died at Otrar in February 1405. His sons and grandsons fought over the succession, and his vast conquests shrank to a Timurid realm in Persia and Central Asia.

events.name: Death of Timur
events.text: Timur died at Otrar and the invasion of China was abandoned.

name: Hussite Wars
summary: After the reformer Jan Hus was burned at the Council of Constance, his Czech followers rose against the Church and Emperor Sigismund, heir to the Bohemian crown. Hussite armies of peasants and townsmen, led by Jan Zizka and later Prokop the Great, used armoured war wagons and handguns to defeat five crusades and raid deep into Germany and Hungary. The movement split, and moderate Utraquist and Catholic nobles destroyed the radicals at Lipany in 1434, opening the way to a compromise with Rome.

steps.label: 1419 to 1420
steps.title: Defenestration and the first crusade
steps.text: In July 1419 radical Hussites threw Catholic councillors from the windows of Prague's New Town Hall, and King Wenceslas IV died weeks later. When his brother Sigismund claimed the throne, the Pope proclaimed a crusade. Jan Zizka led his followers to the new fortress town of Tabor, then back to Prague, where his men beat the crusaders on Vitkov Hill and Sigismund had to retreat.

events.name: Defenestration of Prague
events.text: Hussites threw the town councillors from the windows, starting the revolt.

events.name: Battle of Vitkov Hill
events.text: Zizka's small force drove the crusaders off the heights above Prague.

steps.label: 1421 to 1422
steps.title: War wagons victorious
steps.text: A second crusade from Saxony and the Rhineland fled from Zatec in 1421 as Hussite armies approached. Sigismund then invaded from Moravia and took Kutna Hora, but the blind Zizka broke out of encirclement with his wagon fort and in January 1422 routed the royal army at Nemecky Brod.

moves.commander: Electors of Saxony and the Rhine
moves.label: Second crusade to Zatec

events.name: Battle of Kutna Hora
events.text: Sigismund took the town, but Zizka's wagon fort broke out at night.

events.name: Battle of Nemecky Brod
events.text: Zizka routed the royal army, which lost hundreds drowning in the river.

steps.label: 1424 to 1427
steps.title: Prokop the Great
steps.text: Zizka died of plague in 1424, and the radical armies of Tabor and the Orphans came under the priest Prokop the Great. In 1426 the Hussites destroyed a Saxon army at Usti nad Labem, and in 1427 a third crusade led by Frederick of Brandenburg and Cardinal Beaufort panicked and fled at Tachov before battle was even joined.

events.name: Battle of Usti nad Labem
events.text: The Hussites crushed a large Saxon army.

events.name: Battle of Tachov
events.text: The crusaders fled in panic as the Hussites approached.

steps.label: 1428 to 1433
steps.title: The beautiful rides
steps.text: Now on the offensive, Prokop led great raids, called the beautiful rides, into Silesia, Austria, Hungary, Saxony and Franconia, living off the land and forcing towns to pay ransom. The winter raid of 1429 to 1430 reached the edges of Leipzig, Bamberg and Nuremberg, and in 1433 a Hussite army fighting alongside Poland against the Teutonic Order reached the Baltic.

moves.label: Winter raid into Saxony and Franconia

events.name: Great raid of 1429 to 1430
events.text: Hussite armies plundered Saxony and Franconia and extorted heavy ransoms.

events.name: Hussites reach the Baltic
events.text: The Hussite army filled its flasks with seawater near Gdansk as a sign of victory.

steps.label: 1431 to 1433
steps.title: Domazlice and Basel
steps.text: A fifth crusade of perhaps 100,000 men under Frederick of Brandenburg and Cardinal Cesarini crossed into western Bohemia in August 1431. At Domazlice the crusaders broke and fled when they heard the Hussite wagons and their battle hymn approaching. Unable to win by force, the Church invited the Hussites to the Council of Basel, which in 1433 granted the Utraquist moderates their key demand of communion in both kinds.

events.name: Battle of Domazlice
events.text: The last crusade fled before the battle, abandoning its baggage.

events.name: Compacts of Basel
events.text: The Council granted the moderates communion in both kinds, splitting the Hussites.

steps.title: Lipany
steps.text: The compromise split the Hussites. A league of Utraquist and Catholic lords seized Prague's New Town and met the radical Taborites and Orphans at Lipany in May 1434. Feigning retreat, they lured the radicals out of their wagon fort and destroyed them, killing Prokop the Great; in 1436 Bohemia accepted Sigismund as king.

events.name: Battle of Lipany
events.text: The moderates destroyed the radical Hussite armies and killed Prokop the Great.

name: Wars of the Roses
summary: Two branches of the royal house of Plantagenet, Lancaster and York, fought for the English throne after the weak Henry VI lost France and his mind. Short, bloody campaigns saw the crown change hands repeatedly between Henry VI, Edward IV and Richard III, while great nobles such as Warwick the Kingmaker switched sides. Henry Tudor's victory at Bosworth in 1485 and at Stoke in 1487 ended the wars and founded the Tudor dynasty.

steps.title: First St Albans
steps.text: Richard, Duke of York, shut out of power by Queen Margaret of Anjou and the Duke of Somerset, marched south with the Nevilles, Salisbury and his son Warwick. They caught the king's party in the streets of St Albans, killed Somerset and took control of Henry VI and the government.

events.name: First Battle of St Albans
events.text: York's men broke into the town, killed Somerset and captured the king.

steps.label: 1459 to 1461
steps.title: Wakefield and Towton
steps.text: Open war followed. The Yorkists captured Henry VI at Northampton in 1460, but York himself was killed at Wakefield and Margaret's northern army marched on London. York's son Edward won at Mortimer's Cross, was proclaimed Edward IV in London, and destroyed the Lancastrians at Towton in a snowstorm, the bloodiest battle ever fought on English soil.

events.name: Battle of Wakefield
events.text: Richard of York was killed attacking a larger Lancastrian army.

events.name: Battle of Towton
events.text: Edward IV crushed the Lancastrians in a snowstorm, securing the crown.

steps.label: 1469 to 1471
steps.title: Barnet and Tewkesbury
steps.text: Warwick the Kingmaker fell out with Edward IV, allied with his old enemy Margaret under French sponsorship, and in 1470 drove Edward into exile and restored Henry VI. Edward landed at Ravenspurn in March 1471, killed Warwick at Barnet in the fog, then raced west to catch Margaret's army at Tewkesbury, where her son was killed; Henry VI died in the Tower soon after.

events.name: Battle of Barnet
events.text: Warwick was killed when the Lancastrians mistook their own allies in the fog.

events.name: Battle of Tewkesbury
events.text: The Lancastrian heir Edward of Westminster was killed and the cause seemed finished.

steps.title: Richard III seizes the throne
steps.text: When Edward IV died in April 1483, his brother Richard of Gloucester intercepted the boy king Edward V at Stony Stratford and took him to the Tower, where he and his brother disappeared. Richard was crowned in July. The Duke of Buckingham's rebellion that autumn collapsed in floods and he was executed, while the last Lancastrian claimant, Henry Tudor, waited in exile in Brittany.

events.name: Usurpation of Richard III
events.text: Edward V and his brother vanished in the Tower as Richard took the crown.

events.name: Buckingham's rebellion fails
events.text: Buckingham was betrayed and beheaded at Salisbury.

steps.title: Bosworth
steps.text: With French money and troops, Henry Tudor sailed from Harfleur and landed at Mill Bay near Milford Haven in August 1485, gathering Welsh support on his march through Shrewsbury. Richard III met him near Market Bosworth; when the Stanleys finally intervened against him, Richard was killed charging at Henry, who was crowned Henry VII.

events.name: Battle of Bosworth
events.text: Richard III was killed and Henry Tudor took the crown.

steps.title: Stoke Field
steps.text: Yorkist exiles crowned a boy, Lambert Simnel, in Dublin as Edward VI. Led by the Earl of Lincoln with German mercenaries paid by Margaret of Burgundy and Irish troops, they landed in Furness and crossed the Pennines, but Henry VII destroyed them at Stoke near Newark, the last battle of the Wars of the Roses.

events.name: Battle of Stoke Field
events.text: Henry VII crushed the last Yorkist army, and Lincoln was killed.

name: Siamese-Khmer wars and the sack of Angkor
summary: The Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, founded in 1351 in the lower Chao Phraya valley, fought the declining Khmer Empire for control of mainland Southeast Asia. According to the chronicles Siamese armies took Angkor more than once before King Borommarachathirat II captured and sacked it in 1431. The Khmer court abandoned the great city and moved south toward Phnom Penh, and Ayutthaya became the leading power of the region.

steps.label: c. 1350 to 1351
steps.title: Founding of Ayutthaya
steps.text: The Thai ruler Uthong united the old Mon and Khmer influenced centres of Lavo (Lopburi) and Suphanburi and in 1351 founded Ayutthaya on an island in the Chao Phraya river. Sitting on the main trade route between the interior and the sea, the new kingdom immediately claimed the western lands that had once belonged to Angkor.

moves.label: From Suphanburi to the new capital

events.name: Founding of Ayutthaya
events.text: Uthong was crowned as King Ramathibodi I of a new Siamese kingdom.

steps.label: c. 1352 to 1357
steps.title: First attack on Angkor
steps.text: According to the Ayutthaya chronicles, Uthong's son Prince Ramesuan led an army east and besieged Angkor around 1352, and the city fell after a long siege. Khmer princes recovered their capital within a few years, but the raid showed how far the Khmer had declined.

events.name: First capture of Angkor
events.text: The chronicles record Angkor taken by the Siamese, though the Khmer soon recovered it.

steps.label: c. 1369 to 1394
steps.title: Angkor taken again
steps.text: Ayutthaya kept up the pressure while also forcing Sukhothai to submit in 1378. Ramesuan, now king, marched on Angkor again and according to the chronicles took it around 1393 to 1394, carrying off thousands of captives and placing a son on the Khmer throne. Once more the Khmer drove the Siamese out, but Angkor's western provinces around Chanthaburi and Korat were slipping away.

events.name: Second capture of Angkor
events.text: The chronicles say Ramesuan took the city and deported many of its people.

steps.title: The sack of Angkor
steps.text: King Borommarachathirat II of Ayutthaya invaded again and besieged Angkor for months. In 1431 the city fell; its treasures, Brahmin priests and many of its people were carried off to Ayutthaya, where Khmer court culture shaped Siamese kingship for centuries.

events.name: Sack of Angkor
events.text: Siamese troops took and plundered the Khmer capital after a long siege.

steps.label: 1431 to c. 1434
steps.title: Angkor abandoned
steps.text: King Ponhea Yat judged Angkor too exposed to Siamese attack and moved the court south and east, first to Srei Santhor and then to Phnom Penh at the meeting of the Mekong and Tonle Sap rivers. The temples were left largely to monks and the jungle, and Cambodia would spend the next centuries squeezed between Siam and Vietnam.

events.name: Court moves to Phnom Penh
events.text: The Khmer capital left Angkor for the safer river country to the south.
